newsitem.title: NEW ZEALAND: OPINION - From the Beehive - NZ super accord in chaos.
newsitem.headline: OPINION - From the Beehive - NZ super accord in chaos.

text.p: WELLINGTON, Feb 26 - Pop icon Prince changed his name to a non-verbal hieroglyph and was ever after called "the entertainer formerly known as Prince".
It is tempting to devise a symbol showing political parties flying off in all directions and call it "the agreement formerly known as the superannuation accord" after this week's events.

Alliance leader Jim Anderton has regularly called news conferences to denounce others' policies as threats to the multi-party accord, while always stopping short of announcing its death or the Alliance's withdrawal.

Labour and the Alliance have been able to explain away their positions on scrapping the surtax in the run up to the 1996 election by reference to the clause that allows a progressive tax regime with equivalent effect in its stead. New Zealand First didn't need to, because it was not a party to the accord.
When National, which is a signatory, agreed to a referendum on compulsory super, Anderton went ballistic.

He said it threatened the certainty which the accord was designed to deliver and should instead be a matter for the accord partners. But Labour was more low-key, recognising that it too had agreed to a referendum as part of its failed negotiations with New Zealand First. As a final line of defence Labour argued the accord was not breached as long as the parties stuck to the agreement to support a publicly-provided scheme and voluntary extra savings, as recommended by the Todd report.

What sent Labour into hyperspace this week and prompted a meeting of the accord partners without National (that is Labour, the Alliance and lone United MP Peter Dunne) was National's refusal to campaign against a compulsory scheme as a party -- although the bulk of its MPs will undoubtedly lobby against compulsion in the September postal ballot.
Labour and the Alliance will lobby as parties against compulsory savings. New Zealand First MPs will enthusiastically back it, but it will be a lonely lobby.
Act went into the election with its own form of compulsory scheme but is reviewing its position.

Finance spokesman Rodney Hide left the party's conference to deliver the last rites to compulsion by praising in his maiden speech the pension scheme MPs have voted themselves: "The MPs' scheme is voluntary. I like that part of it best of all."
Neither is the savings industry likely to throw its weight behind compulsion, although there are a few who still see a dollar or a good principle in it.
So the overwhelming weight of opinion in the lead up to the referendum is likely to be negative.
A single-issue referendum normally delivers a low turnout -- although Justice Minister Doug Graham expects it to be higher than an equivalent ballot box poll.
The government used a turnout of 85 percent to cost the ballot. It would be a real surprise if that level, similar to the turnout at a general election, was achieved.
Having announced it will accept a simple majority as binding, whatever the percentage turnout, the government will wear the political fallout from less than ecstatic backing.
But a good turnout in favour would leave Labour and the Alliance attacking a policy that has public backing.

In an impromptu press conference on Tuesday, Labour's finance spokesman Michael Cullen and Anderton signalled their attack, in the event of a yes' vote for compulsion, would be on the credibility of the poll.
"What credibility would it have if there was a 30 percent turnout and only 17 percent -- just over half -- opted for it?" Anderton asked.

The timetable for the referendum is tight. The decision on Wednesday by Jeff Todd's group monitoring the current regime to issue an interim report before the referendum (when it is obliged to actually report in December) will help the educative effort -- the government has budgeted $4 million for a "neutral" publicity campaign.

Warnings in post-election briefing papers that a scheme could take up to three years to implement are being rejected by treasury ministers as typical departmental conservatism. They are, in a word, being told to deliver. -- Newsroom 64 4 473 4746
